newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Nestle expects sales growth in W Africa.
newsitem.headline: Nestle expects sales growth in W Africa.

text.p: A unified customs zone from 1998 in Francophone West Africa should boost sales of Nescafe soluble coffee and other Nestle products made in the region, the company's West and Central Africa manager said.

"Economic union is already beginning and for us it is the future," Nestle's regional managing director Francois Prevot told Reuters. "We also want to enter into new sectors," he added, declining to specify which products or markets.
Nestle sales in West and Central Africa are dominated by Nescafe soluble coffee, Cerelac-brand baby foods and Maggi-brand stock cubes and other food products.
Nestle plans to raise Ivorian Nescafe output from 10,000 tonnes to 11,500 tonnes in 1998/99 (Oct-Sept), when Ivory Coast liberalises coffee marketing prices.

Other Nestle products, such as Nesquik, could also be marketed more in future, Prevot said, while factories like Cerelac in Ghana, which has strengths in cereal and milk products, could specialise more to get economies of scale.

"We are also increasingly exporting more semi-finished (coffee) product," he added, with bulk exports of soluble coffee in containerised lots of almost 400 plastic bags under test for repackaging elsewhere, such as Senegal.
UEMOA, the French acronym for the mainly francophone West African Economic and Monetary Union of eight countries, has been built up over the past three years towards its customs union.
It includes Ivory Coast, Benin, Togo, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea Bissau, Niger and Senegal. Anglophone countries could join in future.
Nestle has one factory each in Senegal -- which finishes Nescafe products from Ivory Coast -- Cameroon and Ghana. South Africa has 12 Nestle factories. One Greek factory also handles Nescafe coffee.
"We can get synergy across our borders and apply uniform prices," said Prevot, adding that customs tariffs of up to 60 percent of product value had already started to fall.
About 95 percent of Ivorian Nescafe is sent to Europe, where consumers generally prefer smoother tasting arabica coffee.
Greece takes 60 percent. Senegal then Ivory Coast were the main black African markets in 1996, taking 800 tonnes and 700 respectively.
"Greeks are one of the biggest robusta consumers in the world and Ivorian coffee has flavour which is unique," he said.
Nestle says its Africa and the Middle East operations are entering a phase of expansion with annual turnover rising by around 15 percent.
Nescafe coffee sales turnover in the UEMOA zone totalled 16 billion CFA francs in 1996 but a single market with 62 million consumers should push up the figure, Prevot said.
"There is no competition (there for Nescafe," said Prevot, who pointed to small granulated coffee producers supplying mainly wealthy Africans. "Africans drink almost only soluble coffee."
Nescafe purchased around 25,000 tonnes of Ivory Coast robusta for processing in 1996 at its plant there.
